utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 25th of March, 2008. My greetings to the Prosecution team. Good morning, Mr. Seselj. And good morning, Witness. Let's first move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just as a preliminary mention one issue about timing. I think the Prosecution had foreseen to have this witness testify for three hours and the next witness for two hours. I understand Your Honours have issued a Scheduling Order the other way around, so you have two hours for this witness and three hours for the next witness. I will endeavour to complete the testimony of this witness in two hours, but I might run into problems with this, so I would ask for Your Honours' indulgence and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, we were told last week, I think Mr. Mundis said this, that the first witness was supposed to be scheduled for Tuesday and the second witness for Wednesday and Thursday. So if the witness is to be heard on Wednesday and Thursday, it would be best to have three hours for the second witness and two hours for the first witness. However, if you believe that this witness can stay and Tuesday and Thursday, and the other only one day we'll move around as you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours, and we try to speed things up as much as possible in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what is your ethnicity? Sorry. I forgot my microphone, I believe. Mr. Witness, what is your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you do military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In what part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Artillery and rocket units, the anti-aircraft defence. A special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And would the usher please call up 65 ter number 2869. Your Honours, this is a map. I'm just waiting for that to come up. Could we zoom in on sort of the middle where we have -- yeah, let's try to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see the town of Zvornik and the town of Karakaj on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is the distance between Zvornik and Karakaj approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it's about three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the area of Karakaj, can you describe that? What is in Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karakaj was an industrial zone with all the factories there. Zvornik was a valley and all the factories and manufacturing plants were in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, we're done with this exhibit. I would like to tender this. We might want to have this in as an exhibit. It's also included --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit number P00302, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you tell us what was the relationship like between Muslims and Serbs when you grew up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Especially -- I'm sorry. The relationship was good. I don't know. I grew up in a house in which this was not an -- important at all. My father was a patriot and 90 per cent of my friends were Serbs, and I still have contacts to many of them to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in which town did you grow up? Maybe I should have asked that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I grew up in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the relationship between Serbs and Muslims changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship started changing let me say when the Serb national consciousness started waking up. I don't know how deep or how far I should go into the matter, but it all started in Gazimestan with various demonstrations, songs that praised the Serb nationality. It all started, but I never believed at the time that this could all end up in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Approximately what year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately we're talking about the relationship which started deteriorating in 1988, albeit slowly. There were first rallies in Kosovo, and the Serbs started singing their songs. I'm talking about rock singers who would become members of the academy of sciences and arts. And this was all part of the plan that had been envisaged by the Serbian academy of sciences and arts. So it went across the board in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving some years ahead to the spring of 1992. Did you live in Zvornik at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there -- were there -- were there signs at the time that there would be an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were signs. First of all, lorries full of reservists were passing through Zvornik. There were all sorts of military convoys. They passed through Zvornik and Mali Zvornik, and those reservists on the way back from the theatres of war would shoot, would fire in the air. But the relationship in the town itself did deteriorate, but they were not so tense as to lead to a conflict because we still socialised amongst ourselves and we all very often joked promising each other that we would guard each other's backs. It was very difficult to imagine that people that you lived with all your life could turn against you, and then on the Karakaj bridge, I don't know, there were political meetings day and night with showdowns of political parties, and on the eve of the war there were some lorries full of reservists who were being taken to Celopek and Rocevic villages for military training. I wanted to see them, and on one occasion I and my neighbour who wanted to buy something, we went there to see whether that was the truth, and really when we went down to Celopek there were a lot of troops there. We stopped for a while. We had a drink, and nobody minded us being there, but they were involved in heavy military training there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when approximately was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was approximately at the beginning of March. Actually, I don't know whether it was at the beginning of March or in mid-March, but in any case it was at the beginning of March because we could not understand that this all might lead to -- to a war in the 20th Century.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see signs that the Serb population in Zvornik was preparing or taking steps because of an upcoming conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as measures are concerned, one weekend before the barricades were put up most of the Serbs were not in Zvornik. They had left. They -- they loaded their cars full of valuables and they went to a village near Zvornik. The reservists were there but nobody counted on a war, on a large-scale war. We thought, okay, even if something happened they would try to take something. Maybe they would fail. We would be able to defend ourselves, and that was our line of thinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I have a follow-up question. You're telling us that the Serbs left Zvornik. Now, to your knowledge did they leave Zvornik because they were ordered to leave town or was it a spontaneous move because they were afraid, because when you're afraid you just flee, or could there be a third reason behind this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that it was a dress rehearsal. I believe that they had all received orders, because it would really be strange or even impossible that so many of them were not there. And if I may add to that, some of my good friends with whom I still socialised, because there was no reason for us not to socialise, I heard comments to the effect, "This is not boding well. We don't know what's happening."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you see any military equipment being stationed so as to be defending or in a position to defend the bridges over the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Karakaj bridge there was a tank. It was put there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was that before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, did -- to your knowledge were steps taken on the Muslim side to somehow prepare for a conflict and, if so, were you yourself involved in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no organised measures in place. People organised themselves spontaneously. Everybody tried to protect their families and themselves the best way they could. During the night, for example, in town, because there were rumours about various incidents, people started keeping guard spontaneously in the street because they were afraid. And the guards were mixed until the very last moment. We just tried to protect ourselves or alert others to possible danger. I personally, when I heard and saw what was going on, I also undertook some security measures. My house was next to the forest, and that's why I purchased a Kalashnikov automatic weapon on the black market in order to protect myself and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lended that automatic weapon to the others who were standing guard to be able to protect themselves if attacked. As for any other type of organisation there was nothing in place. People just spontaneously went out to the street, took up weapons, and tried to protect themselves and their families. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, sorry. I'm just waiting to allow for the translation to come through. I know it's a bit artificial as a discussion, but we have to do it this way. Do you remember any media reportings about the situation in Zvornik prior to the attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a order, activity in order to find a measure to avoid war. Nobody really wanted war, because war means suffering. The day before the first shots were fired in Zvornik, on Belgrade TV a report was aired according to which there had been sporadic shooting in Zvornik and allegedly there were 11.000 Green Berets on the Kula tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to those Green Berets a bit later, but where were you when the attack on Zvornik started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did you first learn about the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father woke me up. He was obviously scared, and he told me there's shooting. Still half a sleep I said, "No. It's impossible. You're imagining things. It's in your head." And he said, "No, no. There is shooting going on." Then I got up and I really heard from the direction of Karakaj shots being fired. You know, it's a new feeling, a new thing, and it's a mixture of fear and curiosity that brought me outdoors. I wanted to see what was going on. I could hear shots from the direction of Karakaj and Vidakova Njiva, and then a total of three shells fell. They started falling, and I believe that there were three altogether. And then cannon fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the cannon fire hit -- hit the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the vicinity of my house one shell fell on the house of Pero the painter who was a Serb. That's what I know about one of them. I don't know about the other two and whether they did any damage. The rest were -- was cannon fire, which was open, but they tried to spare the town because I believe that the intention was to preserve as much of the town before they took over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you're telling about a shell. Does this mean that there was artillery fire before the forces entered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That shell fell. I don't know where it was fired from. I'm not a military expert. And then the artillery fire was opened just to instill fear. There were detonations all the time. There were explosions all the time, and the feeling we had was that we were really in war, and this created a great deal of panic among the population, and people would just grab their children, get into their cars, start fleeing. Those who were closer to the bridge started fleeing towards Serbia, and those who were a bit further away from the bridge started running towards Kula and Divic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did I understand you correctly that you went outside? Just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see any of the attacking forces or could you only hear them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first we could only hear them. A few of us neighbours gathered amongst the houses. We were standing there. And at one point bullets started flying, and we could see a sniper shooting in our direction from one of the high-rise buildings. And then we started running. We took shelter behind a different house. We were happy that nothing had happened to us. We were also a bit afraid and in order to diminish that fear I told a neighbour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, in the French translation you talked about a sniper who had a Z-16, but the -- in the English version the type of weapon has not been mentioned. Could you please confirm that there was a sniper using a weapon that -- for which you gave us the characteristics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall and as far as I was able to observe, there were only snipers on the buildings. It was very hard at that distance, which must have been at least 800 metres to 1 kilometre, using ordinary military weapons to target with such precision. I couldn't see that he was a sniper, but because the shots were fired with such precision we assumed he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of weapon did the sniper have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of weapon this was I couldn't tell you. All I know is that we saw that from that building a man holding a rifle fired shots. It didn't look like an automatic rifle as far as we could tell, and we assumed that he was a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The -- am I understanding your answer correctly? You didn't see the forces that were approaching from Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you -- have you -- had you heard before the attack what forces were at Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had. I hadn't seen them, but I did hear about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: From who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arkan's men, Seselj's men, and the several local adherents were standing, were manning the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that from several sides and also my father told me he had been stopped at the check-point and checked. He recognised them. One sort had cockades on their heads and wore beards, and the others had insignia on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- getting back to the attack. So you were being targeted by a sniper. You ran away. You were sitting in another position. Were you then being shot at again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I joked with that neighbour of mine, and I said to him, "Have you found time to get married?" "Well, at least I had time to have a honeymoon, but you don't." He then gave me a little push and he said, "Do you still care about that?" And as he gave me a little push, at that point where my head had been a bullet landed. We were sheltering behind the houses, and we started running.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This is a question of a technical nature. You were talking to your neighbour, and at that moment he jolts you and you realise that there was a bullet impact. How were you dressed then? Were you in civilian clothes? Were you wearing a camouflage uniform? How were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wearing my leather jacket, jeans, and shoes. Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then you -- you started running. And just because we have limited time, where did you ultimately go to on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I began to run. I was first, and I arrived at a fence. A woman had put up a fence around her vegetable garden. It was a wooden fence. I couldn't get through, and I was so frightened that I managed to pull out the planks. I threw myself down on the ground. Bullets kept whizzing around us. I could feel pebbles and bits of earth flying around my head, but fortunately they didn't hit us. And then we saw that that sniper was shooting from the line pit. We crawled along and managed to get out along the road going to Kula Grad along which everyone was fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you go to Kula Grad yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you go back to Zvornik after of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On that night I returned to Zvornik, but I went back to my house to get some things with some of the neighbours who had forgotten to take some things with them. We heard shooting from all sides, and that night we went back to Kula Grad through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you -- did you then returning to Kula Grad the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night, in the course of the night, we went back to Kula Grad. We spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you have your rifle when you were in Kula Grad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But that morning my father took me with him, and I handed the rifle to a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you were in Kula Grad did you see 11.000 Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's ridiculous. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There were some people who in one way or another managed to get weapons. There were a few reserve policemen, and to the best of my recollection that was all. There may have been as many as 40 armed men that I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was Kula Grad defended, so to speak, for -- for a while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Kula Grad was defended. On that first morning I left. I went with my father to a hamlet to stay with some relatives, and then I saw that they didn't really have a lot of food. So I went to Divic. I spent a few days there. Then I went back to that hamlet again, and then I went back to Kula Grad a day before it fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I hope I may be allowed to lead on this point, it should be a matter of no controversy. Am I correct that Kula Grad has a hill, and on top of that hill is an old fortress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was that the position that was defended for a while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There where the old fortress is, and in another part where there is the village. The whole village, together with the old fortress, was defended. If I may, I would like to add that on that first day -- or, rather, that morning when I fled to that hamlet with my father, tanks from Serbia shot at Kula Grad. There were three tanks located in Mali Zvornik. But as the fortress was very big and strong, not much damage was done. I don't know how many shots were fired, but I do know that they fired shots and we were afraid. When I was at Divic, you could see very well where they were and how they were shooting and how the stones were flying around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, when -- when Kula Grad fell, did you try to flee and, if so, where were you trying to flee to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did try to flee, yes. It was hell. There was firing from all sides. We had no weapons, so a friend of mine and I started to flee. On the other side of Kula Grad tanks were moving in the direction of Tuzla, and therefore we started running towards the village of Kamenica. People were fleeing. It was like a war movie. Everybody took whatever possessions they could. They put them on a horse or in a car. They would take their children, and they would all flee. We fled also. We went in the direction of Kamenica. They kept shelling us constantly. That night we arrived in a big village called Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but did you ultimately try to reach Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We intended to, but a group of people who had been at Kula Grad and had weapons managed to break through to Tuzla, but we didn't dare. There was shooting coming from that side and we saw tanks on that side and houses burning there. So we didn't dare go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you -- could you describe the areas you moved through just in a general way. Did you see any villages in the areas you passed through and, if so, had there been attack on those villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a village behind Kula Grad. I didn't know those villages very well before the war, but I learned later on this village is called Marchcici, a village or a hamlet or something. I don't know what it is exactly. And there were houses burning up there and from there a tank was firing at Kula. This was on higher ground than Kula was. And we fled down to Josanica and there were several villages there, several hills. People fled. There were groups of refugees. And we would come across copses of trees and wooded areas where people were hiding, elderly people, children. We came across a group of people who were fighting at Kula or had been fighting at Kula, and they had a wounded man with them who died later on. Everybody in those villages was packing up. Houses were beginning to burn. And from the hills we could see all those villages and everybody packed up and started fleeing in the direction of Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ultimately were you captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you with anyone when you were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were five of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you give us the name, the name of the four others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we move into private session, because I don't want to reveal my identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel. Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sir, what will dates approximately were you captured, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 4th of May. 1992, yes. The day when Tito died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we have to skip ahead in the story a bit. And maybe -- were you later in that day taken to a place where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later we were -- shall I go in chronological order or do you just want me to tell you where we ended up that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think in the interest of time we just have to go to where you ended up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We ended up in Standard, a former footwear factory in Zvornik, in the building of the management on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you get closer to the microphone, please, when you speak, because it's difficult for the interpreters to hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter number 4052. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is this the Standard shoe factory?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I've been quite patient, Mr. President, especially when we were dealing with personal family relations and I didn't want to object when leading questions were put, but with respect to this photograph, the proper question would be, "What is this," and not, "Is this this or that." So please tell the Prosecutor to examine properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Marcussen, just show the photograph and ask him what's on the photograph. I know that you tried to gain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I thought these matters were not disputed by the accused, but -- do you know what this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Standard footwear factory, but we were looked up in the management building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And can that part of the factory be seen on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. No, you can't really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you still with your four friends at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where were you placed in the management building or the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put us on the second floor. When you stand in front of the building that's the second floor on the left-hand side. As you go up the stairs where you enter the building, you go up to the second floor, it's to the right and then the door of that big room is straight ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The room that you were taken into, were there any other people detained there when you came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First they searched us, then they took us in. Inside the room there were some people I knew. Some were from Divic and others were from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When your searched, were anything taken from you or were you just searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the SUP station in Zvornik they confiscated my gold bracelet and gold chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Am I correct that this is in the part of the chronology that we jumped over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So at the Standard factory they just did another check of you, but nothing was taken from you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So what -- you were searched and then things were taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They searched us and then they took us inside that room, and then a military policeman arrived. I don't remember what his rank was. They called him Mrki, and first he took away two people to give statements. After that he came back and took me and a friend of mine to write statements. When we entered the room there was a piece of paper there and a pencil. He paced up and down the room and he told us to write down where and when we were born, why were born, and where we had been from the time the shooting started until today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you gave a statement were you in any way mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He told us that he was a decent man, that he wasn't going to beat anyone, but if somebody came and asked us if we had been beaten we should say that we had been kicked in the kidneys or beaten in the kidneys, and then he rattled the door and we made some noise to make it sound as if he was beating us, but he didn't actually touch us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But did he say he had received instructions to beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did. He said he had been issued with orders to beat everyone who had been brought in while questioning them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The people that were guarding the prisoners at the Standard factory, how did they look? What kind of -- were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing olive-grey, drab uniforms of the sort worn by the JNA, and the white straps worn by the police. The military police, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know who their chief was at the Standard factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be a hundred per cent certain, but judging by the way they behaved in certain situations I would say it was Niski. I can't be absolutely certain whether that was actually correct and whether it related to the entire military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This person, Niski, how did you learn his -- his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what everyone called him. I'm not aware that he harmed anyone throughout my stay there. In my opinion -- or, rather, I heard some people say he was Arkan's man. Others said he was Seselj's man. I believe he was Arkan's man, but he always tried to protect the prisoners as far as we could tell. I don't know what happened elsewhere, in other places, I wasn't there, but he's the only one I can really have a good opinion of, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is Niski a real name or is that a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's a nickname everybody used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While you were in the Standard factory were you given any work to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We cleaned the rooms. Various units were stationed there. I think there was the sabotage units on one side, the reconnaissance men on another. When you went up onto the first floor to the right were the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness slow down, please. This is too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The interpreters ask you to speak a little slower because they have difficulties keeping up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think -- could you just tell us once again what units were there, because I think that got lost. If you would repeat that part of your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were reconnaissance men and sabotage men on the ground floor. On the first floor there were people from Loznica because we brought gets in for them, and the military police. I think it was the military police, yes. And on the second floor, as you went up the stairs on the right-hand side were we prisoners, and on the left-hand side were Seselj's men from Kraljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll go more into the identity of these -- a number of these different units and members of them, but I think the time for the break might be coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We're missing a player.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Very well. So the hearing is resumed. Mr. Marcussen, if I understood you right, you told us you needed three hours with this witness and two hours with the next one. So the -- of course you're using three hours, which means that Mr. Seselj will also be given three hours for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: T0hank you, Your Honours. Before I continue, I would like to tender the photograph of the Standard factory, that was 4052. I forgot to ask for an exhibit number for that one I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number P00303. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, instead of having the Prosecutor find us the photograph of the administrative building of Standard so that that can be an exhibit, because the witness actually said that the prisoners were put up in the administrative building of the Standard factory and that there were either members of the army there or whoever, now he's sending us a photograph which is completely irrelevant. So if they don't have the photograph of the administrative building they can send somebody to take a photograph. I don't know why this is being tendered at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently you do not have the photograph of the administrative building. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in -- did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you gave the statement did you make a number of sketches to indicate various locations you had been in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And those sketches, did you sign and date them when you had drawn them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to call up Exhibit number 2208.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, I can see that several times on several occasions you very pedantically intervened when the Prosecutor asked the witness to identify something that had been previously marked on the photograph. You stepped in. Now the Prosecutor is presenting something which the witness at one time long ago drew. I think that that is impermissible regardless of the fact that it doesn't have any effect as far as I'm concerned, maybe it's an authentic rendition. I have no reason to doubt the fact because what the witness has said so far is in order, but I think that this is impermissible, because since 1996 it's been 12 years, and the OTP staff had an opportunity of photographing everything, drawing up precise sketches and then putting that to the witness so that the witness could identify them in precise terms, not to have a sketch which is 12 years old presented here for the witness to identify it now. So let's hear from the Prosecutor first how this sketch was made in the first place. Was it an aerial view or where this was sketched from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness drew this sketch on the 29th of September, 1996. I suppose that the investigator who was with him and whose name must be in the statement, Mazhar Inayat was the name of the investigator, he must have asked the witness to locate the administrative building as well as the various individuals and units. They didn't have any photograph. If they had any photographs, it would have been much easier, and so the witness drew this himself. We are interested in knowing who was on the right-hand side on the second floor. That's the most relevant for you. So, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let me first ask you is this something that -- is this a sketch that you remember making?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I can see there is some handwriting on it in -- in your language, and there's some handwriting in English. Who made -- who wrote in -- the things that are written in your language on the sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the things that are written in English, who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the investigator when he asked me subsequent questions, and then by -- based on the explanations he would add the floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there is a cross marked in the -- what I believe is the administrative building. There is a box with a cross in it. What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's where we prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what is written next to the cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "Prisoners" in abbreviated form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then where is a number 1, what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the Seselj's men and the Kraljevcani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rosnica Nidi [phoen], war -- military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 3 was the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Number 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reconnaissance men and the others were the sabotage people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you say the others is that number 5, or what is number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Number 5 were sabotage or diversionary forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, how did you know that all these people were on the ground floor or on the first floor and you yourself being on the second floor? Well, we can understand where you were since you were a prisoner, but how did you know that there was this sabotage unit located on the ground floor? How did you know all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was taken to clean up the premises, the building, a few times, and at every entrance to these premises or rooms it would say "Diversionary," "Military police," "War police," "Reconnaissance" and so on up on the doors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seselj's men, was that mentioned on a piece of paper too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't say that there, but they were their rooms. I know that because they would go there. They would visit us from time to time. And then they took out one of my friends for interrogation. So that's where their rooms were, but I didn't go in there to clean them. But I did go into all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Later on during your stay at the Standard factory and locations that we're going at that talk about later on, did you -- did you have a chance to learn more about the identity of the group of Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please? I'm not sure I understood it. I don't think the lady -- you're interested in the identities that I learnt then or that I learn about later on, which?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No. My question is did you -- apart from knowing about this particular room when you were in the Standard factory, did you interact or were you in close contact with men from the -- from Seselj's group at various times throughout the events we're going to discuss today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Yes. Major Toro came by, and he took video footage of us. We had to give our first and last names and where we were from. And later on I heard that that record was broadcast over television Serbia, and it said that a diversionary group had been captured which tried to infiltrate itself into Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphone and speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They observed us. They would come by and observe us. They didn't beat us. Vojvoda Cele came by once. I think that at that point he had one or two knives hitched onto his belt, and he was laughing and kept touching the knife. And then Sasa from the Kraljevo group came by once, too, and he said, "A special man would come by. He will talk to you. You mustn't look him in the eyes, and you must address him with Vojvoda, sir, honourable Vojvoda sir, and if any of you knew who conducted what machinations in Zvornik and what business that they should tell him," and one of us stepped forward, and he went to those rooms, to those premises and stayed there for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you gave a statement in 1996, that statement, have you had a chance to review that again before you have given testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an occasion to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in the statement do you give a description of various members of the Loznica group and the group of Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course to the best of my recollection, as I saw them. And in principle, I always tried to determine their height judging by my own height give or take 20 centimetres. So it was what I saw with my own eyes, roughly my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in preparing for your testimony today, were you shown an extract from your statement which is a list of these various members of the two groups that you have identified in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you have and opportunity to look at the list to see if the list was accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you make some corrections to the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollections. And as far as I remember after such a long period of time, of course, to the extent that is possible that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher to assist me showing the witness -- you can show this copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, the witness is now being given a document not that he signed but that was compiled by the OTP allegedly on the basis of his statement, and now the witness is being led to repeat what he said about these nicknames. I think that is absolutely impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Actually, this particular list a signed by the witness. It was -- the list itself has -- is in the system and has been disclosed to the accused, and it has 65 ter number 7184. During the proofing - and this is what I was going to ask the witness about - the witness have as he said reviewed the list and has made certain corrections to the list based on his memory. He has signed this list and he has signed and dated each of the corrections he has made, and I was going to ask the witness to confirm his signature and tender this document into evidence. So that's what I was going to do, and I don't think there's a basis for the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, if I understand you properly, in his prior statement he described six members of the Seselj's men, Vojvoda Cele, Major Toro, Pufta, Zoks, Sasa, and Sava, and you listed all of the descriptions in this document together with some minor corrections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What we have done is we have, yes, isolated from the list and the statement what is the description, taken out anything which is -- and there were just a very few bits which are not mere descriptions. So we only have descriptions of these persons. And then the witness has reviewed the list, confirms that this corresponds to his memory. He has signed the list yesterday, and because he had some amendments and additions, he have written those additions on the list and signed it. The list is composed of two parts. It has the so-called Loznica group, which is also relevant to the case, and then we have the group of Seselj's -- so-called Seselj's men. This is measure to try to be able to get through their identity quickly. I'm happy to go through this with the witness as live evidence before the witness starts looking at the list again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This list bear the Exhibit number 2195. So it is the amended list compared to the initial prior statement, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I believe the exhibit number in your folder is 7184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Yes. I was wrong. Yes, 7184. What are the details that he changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe I should distribute to Your Honours as well a copy. I wanted to lay a foundation first with the witness, but we can also do it the other way round. If the usher would assist. As all this was done last night, I'm afraid the amendments and translations are in -- in handwriting. Sorry, I -- we have copies for everyone, for the Judges and for the accused. So if Your Honours look at the bottom of the first page you will see there's a signature and a date. And if Your Honours turn to the second page you will see corrections being made and in the English version you can see what those corrections are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that this is scandalous. First I don't seem to have that number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do not say that this is scandalous or a scandal. There is an investigator. He met with the witness in 1996, in September 1996, and this investigator asked the witness to describe the individuals he saw when he was sweeping the floors or the individuals who were in those premises. Back then the witness told us the story and gave an exact description, as far as he could see, of those individuals. For instance, Vojvoda Cele. He was the leader of the group from Kraljevo. He was 172 centimetres tall, weighed about 100 kilos, and he had a big stomach, shoulder length black hair, et cetera. So these are the kind of details provided by the witness. And during proofing the witness added some corrections, only a few of them, and these are to be found on page 2 of the English version and on page 2 of the B/C/S version. That's all. So please do not say that this is a scandal. This is merely a means of eliciting identification information on the individuals who were there. And rather than saying that this is a scandal, I draw your attention to the paragraph regarding Major Toro. He seemed to have a military ID, so that could be a clue to the fact that he might have ban JNA member. So before you criticise, listen first to the Prosecution's questions. You will have the cross-examination in order to crush this if you want. We are now trying to understand how this presence of these people was in the administrative building. The witness is saying that there were some of Seselj's men in that building, and we are trying now to find out who these people are. So please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, am I correct that you have made corrections and you have signed this document where you made the corrections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Now you're tolerating something amazing, an amazing leading question. Whether the Prosecutor's right. Well, of course the Prosecutor is always right in front of this Tribunal and that's not a scandal I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It has already been stated several times by both the president, and you yourself brought up the issue, it has already been said that the document is signed. We are really get into silly formalities here. There is no problem with a leading question in this context. And the witness has signed the pseudonym sheet and we can compare straight away his signature on the pseudonym sheet and the signature on his statement. This is just a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a waste of time because the witness signed the document thereby authenticating the changes that he made, and these are really minor changes. Please proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just in terms of the basis for your description, when you have described these people you have listed, is that based only on what you saw at the Standard factory or did you subsequently see these people in places where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This relates to my entire stay there. Well, in different concentration camps or different places. It was on the basis of everything that I drew my conclusions. And then if I was able to stand by them, then I would sort of try and remember how tall they were, how much they weighed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when were you ultimately released from what you refer to as concentration camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 4th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So did I understand your answer correctly to be that from May until December 1992 you on a number of occasions had opportunity to see these people maybe, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Until July, the 15th of July. That's when we were transported to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, July, yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we first of all ascertain who were the so-called Seselj's men that he saw in the Standard shoe factory, because otherwise I'm a bit lost. Does this list correspond to the entire period? We were talking about the shoe factory. Can we stick to that and see what this witness knows about the so-called Seselj's men who were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I'm going to just do a few more questions about the identification, and then as we go through Your Honours will see a number of these names appearing in different contexts over the period of time that we have just been discussing, some of them at the Standard factory, some of them at other locations that we're going too talk about. But I think it's useful to introduce these people at this stage so we all know who we're dealing with, and then we will cover their actions as we move through. So I'll get to this in just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we -- as we've been talking about the group of Seselj's men, now you say about Toro that he had a military ID that identified him as one of Seselj's men, or Seselj's army as it says in the English translation. Did you see the ID at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see the military ID. My friend told me he had seen one. And later on while I was working -- or looting for them in town, actually, at one point when Major Toro gave Pufta lots of money, passed over lots of money by standing beside a truck that was going to Kraljevo and told him what to do, he gave him a black ID card on which, I think in silver letters, I'm not sure whether they were silver or gold letters, but anyway, there was a cockade on it, and it said "Serbian Radical Party." So I assumed that it was some sort of ID card. It was like the ID cards we had. Whether it was a proper ID card or something else I can't say with certainty because I was standing on the truck and loading up, actually, and I saw this wad of notes. You know, you can see when somebody hands a wad of notes to somebody else. So that's what happened. He said, "Take this, and you know what you're supposed to do."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And with respect to Sasa and Sava, do you know whether they held any -- did you ever hear about them holding a rank within Seselj's group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember about Sasa, but of Sava I know -- well, I think this was in June. They talked and said he had been promoted, that Seselj was in Zvornik and that he had promoted Sava to the rank of major. That's what Zoks and Pufta said. And Sava said that there was a celebration and that the other two were promoted to captain. Zoks and Pufta. Zoks and Pufta. Pufta and Zoks. They were also promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you yourself overheard that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And Zoks is a friend of mine. Because -- he congratulated him, and the other one thanked him, said thank you -- "I congratulate you on your promotion." And he said, "Thank you, thank you."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say, "He's a friend of mine." Did you know him beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. That was a poor interpretation. I didn't say he was my friend, but my friend congratulated him on his promotion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that it's very difficult to hear the witness. Could he please speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I know it's difficult, but you need to try to speak a bit louder because there's a difficulty in hearing what you're saying. The -- on your list you have a Loznica group. Did you know members of this group before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How did you know them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew them because us guys would go to Loznica frequently and they would come to Zvornik from time to time, and it's a group of people who were known to the police. They had thick dossiers. So when you arrive in a town, for instance, then in principle you always try to learn who -- whom you should avoid, and those were the people. So you did your best to say hello to them, pay them a round of drinks so that they wouldn't touch you. So as I say, we knew one another by sight. I actually knew one of them, if I can put it this way, the leader, Stuka, I knew him a little better, not very well, but we would even have a drink from time to time. I knew him through a girl that we knew. I don't want to enter into any intimate details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This particular group, do you know who their leader was in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stuka would always bring them, but their real leader was Gogic. That's what they said. That's what we heard. Gogic did not come, but once when we were loading up he had a red Golf car, he took us with him so that we could load up some things that he took a fancy to for his flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you -- did you ever overhear a conversation which informed you about who they reported to outside the Standard factory? Sort of higher up the chain, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who did they report to first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we're coming to the day when they beat us, these people from Loznica, the Loznicani, then Niski stormed in, he stopped the beating and argued with them, and then Stuka told him, "If something's not clear to you, go and see Major Marko Pavlovic because he's the only one I receive orders from."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And do you know what position Marko Pavlovic held in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I learnt from what the guards said amongst themselves, he was the chief of the town defence at the time, as far as I understood it. The Serbian defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could just go in for one question in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before we round this off, there's into dispute about the name, but there is dispute about the Prosecutor's precision and his knowledge of the case. The dispute about the name has been resolved. It has been resolved here before this OTP and before the court in Belgrade. There's nothing in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's on the record. Let's move to open session unless we already are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record we are back in open session. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need an order in order to redact line -- the lines that deal with the person tried in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It looks to me that that was said while we were still in private session. No? No... we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really know. Only the registrar can tell us. Open session on line 12, page 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think that the mere mention of the identity of this -- it's not a concern for this case. If Your Honour is concerned about the identity of the accused before the war crimes chamber in Belgrade, but this as itself we don't need a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Chamber would rather redact just to be extra careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I think we have to skip ahead. On the fifth day you were in the Standard factory were -- were you mistreated on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were. On the fifth day of our stay there the people from Loznica came. Loznicani as they were known. Stuka brought them in and asked if anybody knew him. We lowered our heads, although some of us did know him, and then he said, "Okay. Nobody knows him." Then they lined themselves, distributed themselves, and they started beating us. One whom I knew as Dejan stood next to me and said, "I'll take this one." He hit me several times, and obviously there was one with his pistol out of the holster guarding us if any of us tried to defend ourselves. After I suffered a few blows, although I had never practised any martial arts, he said, "This one seems to be a hard nut to crack." And then one of the boxers came. He hit me, and then I flew across the room like in the movie. They were beating us. They took turns. I would highlight the especially cruel persons who beat us. His name was Lale, one of the Loznica guys. He forced me to take off my shoes and socks, and then he beat me using a very thick electricity cable. He beat me on the soles of my feet, and he asked me whether it hurt, and I was crying out in pain. I said that it did hurt a lot, and then he said, "This does not hurt. This just drives you insane." And then I would also like to highlight another person from the Loznica group. His name -- rather nickname was Macak. He sported a mustache. He came to us. He grabbed us by the loins and then -- I'll try and demonstrate it with my own hands. That's how he grabbed us by the loins, and then he would twist our loins backwards. And there was another person standing in front of us hitting us with a boxer all the time. Stuka was telling them all this time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When this movement was being done to you, were you being hit at the same time? Is that what you're saying? One would hold you and another one would hit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was it, and it was very painful because you were -- your body was twisted backwards, and then another person would run up to you and hit you. And all this time Stuka was ordering them not to hit us in the head. Whoever was crying or screaming, they would throw him on the ground. They would push them against the ground with their knees, and then they would hit them with police baton. There was a girl with them. She was barefoot. She had a dark brown or black hair, long. She sported a pony-tail. And she must have been into martial arts, and she was using us as -- as sparring partners or punching bags. She did not hit me. This lasted all the night. The first time they left, let me say this, they gave us a pencil --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Let me just stop you. You described that Lale hit you under your feet. Did he also hit you in other places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He also hit me, and I forgot to say that he hit me on the left knee and the leg above the left knee. So my foot -- my leg went numb. I stopped feeling my leg. He was beating me on the one and the same place all the time. So my leg went completely numb. I could not feel my leg. I tried to protect it with my hand, but I couldn't. I could just feel tingles passing through my leg, and I can still have -- feel the same sensation sometimes in my left leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You said you were given -- eventually the beating stopped and you were given a piece of paper. Now, were you the only one being beaten or were all of you in the room beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody, yes, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how many of you were there in the room at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six. I believe that there were eight of us, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how long did the beating last for, the period -- the thing you just have talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted until they were worn out. I can't give you the exact time. The first time they gave us pencils to write what we knew about similar people from Zvornik with criminal records, and then at that moment when they were worn out Niski would come. He would interrupt them. He would enter into arguments with them. And he told us that this would not repeat again, and we told him that we had been given pencils and papers to write, and he said we did not have to do it. An hour or two hours later they returned and they started beating us again following the same scenario, and finally when they were tired Niski came back, argued with them, and then he yelled at the guards. And then what -- by that time we had already written on those papers what we knew and what we didn't know. The third time they came we hoped that they would not beat us because we had filled those papers, and I would not want to repeat before the Trial Chamber what they told us. Stuka tore up the papers, said he was not interested in that, and the last time we were beaten. Towards the morning Niski came and apologised for everything that had been done and he pleaded with us not to tell about the whole event. We agreed hoping that that would stop any further beating. And then he said that we would be released, that he had made some inquiries about us in the meantime and that we would be released. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Let me stop you there. When you were repeated -- you were repeatedly beaten, how many times did people come back and beat you, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe five times but I'm not sure, but this was repeated. I'm not a hundred per cent sure. I don't know. Three, maybe five or so. I don't know. I believe it was five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were the beating of the same nature each time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time of the same nature. Some of them adopted their own pets to put it that way, and they would approach that person immediately. Obviously that's how they functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was it the -- was it the same group that came back and beat you each time or were there different groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night just that group returned. And Niski even yelled at the guards, trying to tell them that they should not let that group in, that they should use their arms, but it failed every time. They all returned again and again and beat us. And that morning they put us in a mini van. They took us to in front of the building of the military department in Zvornik. We were driven by a military police. Mrki was among them as the person who interviewed us first. He apologised to us, said he could not do anything about that. There's something I forgot to tell you. After the last round of beating, the guys from Loznica told us, "We shall meet you later today at the Ekonomija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You had also said that Niski had said that you would be released. So what happened? Did you actually go to Ekonomija or were you released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They brought us to the building of the military department. They started handing out passes. The group from Loznica came, took those passes from us, and they ordered the military police to take us to Ekonomija. While we were at the Standard we heard all the worst things about Ekonomija. The guards kept telling us that whoever went to Ekonomija did not come from there alive and that's what we feared the most. When we arrive at Ekonomija they took our belts, shoelaces, personal IDs, and whatever jewellery people had on them, and we could hear guards comment, saying, "Well, you won't need those any more anyway." And then they took us into the Ekonomija building. Ekonomija is actually a farm building near Zvornik, and I believe that the room that we were in had served as a storage. It was rather high. It had a window high up with bars on it. It had a metal door. It was -- it had a concrete floor. And on the door, on the metal door, there was a small opening through which we could be handed food. When they brought us there, there were between 15 and 20 people there but I can't be exactly sure of the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let's just have a look maybe at exhibit number -- 65 ter number 4147. Mr. Witness, are you -- can you tell us if you know what this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the building at the Ekonomija in Karakaj. Next to the large, big building is that smaller building where we were kept. I'm talking about the small building of which you can only -- see only the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, again this is the best picture we have, so before we get an objection, I should just mention that. Your Honours, before I forget, I would like to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P00304. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd also like to tender because I think I omitted that 65 ter number 2208. That was the sketch from standard.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P00305. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then, now that we are in this admin business, I'd like to tender 7184. That is a list of Seselj's men and the Loznica men. What I propose to do is to keep the 65 ter number but upload into e-court the amended version that we showed today in court. But if we have an exhibit number for it already now then we can just do that change later.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P00306. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were taken into the room. There were 15 to 20 other people there at the time. At the time when you came to the room did you know the name of any of the these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew a few people there, and I actually got to know all of them during my stay there. I learned their names. But before that I already knew some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let's -- maybe I could ask that we go into private session so the witness can say the identity of the people that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you were in Ekonomija were the -- were prisoners being beaten there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Ekonomija was the hardest period of my incarceration. I would not wish that experience upon anybody, even the worst enemy as our people like to say it. Whoever wanted to beat people would come to Ekonomija. It was a large farm away from the town, a bit away from the road. So you could spend three days there without anybody knowing that you were there. It was just the ideal place for anybody to do whatever they wanted to do to the people there. We were regularly beaten at the Ekonomija farm. The Loznica group came most frequently, and they beat us every time. A person that they referred to as Roki started coming with the Loznica group. I was convinced that in my first statement I mentioned that he had been in training, because later on during my stay when he came alone he would inflict so much damage, there would be so much blood as if there had been five or six of them beating us. Sometimes people from Kraljevo also came, but it was most often people from Loznica who came, the Loznicani group. They came at different times, during the day, during the night. And as for the place where we were incarcerated, I don't know what to tell you. We did not have anything to lie on, just a few cardboards. And one night they even poured water on the floor so that we would not be able to sit or lie down and we... I managed to sleep on my feet, in a sort of semi-conscious state. And you never knew... they would come at random times, day and night, and beat us up. And they even forced us to beat each other. On the second day of my stay at Ekonomija my shoulder was broken. It was done by Roki from Rocevici. I don't know whether he was actually from there or not. I was beaten by two men, and I could only see him running up to me with an intention to kick me in the head. I moved, which angered him. He went outside, took a very wide stake that was prepared for the fence around Ekonomija. He came back and he started beating me with that stake on the showed year and he kept on beating me until I no longer felt my shoulder. I fainted three times. There must have been water in the room because every time he poured water over my head and every time he cursed my mother. And let me not repeat those curses. And he kept on telling me, "You won't die yet, not yet." Finally he asked me, "Do you want me to start beating you on the right shoulder as well?" And I said yes, do that. And then he started beating me with that stake on the right shoulder. He hit me several times, and then he said, "The right shoulder is somewhat sweeter," and then he continued beating me on the left shoulder. He said, "The left shoulder is sweeter." I don't know for how long this lasted for. I only know that he actually broke that thing on my shoulder. He broke my shoulder, and I still suffer the consequences of that beating. I can't lift my left arm, and I have only 30 per cent of the strength of the right arm in my left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me just -- you say you can't lift your left arm. Can you show the court how much you can lift your arm. So the witness is showing that he can only lift his arm a little below horizontal level. And that's the left arm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't lift it any further up because this is where it was broken and it healed incorrectly. The bone healed incorrectly. I don't know how I mustered the strength the following morning, and I'm skipping a few things here because there was an agreement between Cele and Niski that we would be taken to work the following morning. Whoever was able to lift their -- both arms could go to work and if they couldn't then tough luck, and I mustered the strength to lift both my arms and that's how I was taken to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let's just stop for one minute. So the person who was beating on the shoulder, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roki.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what -- what group did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you which group he belonged to. He came with the group from Loznica. Sometimes he would come on his own. At the beginning when he started arriving, he had a spiral -- a frizzy mini-wave, long hair. His hair was bleached. It was originally brown. And then later on when we saw him his hair was short, black, and he also sported a black moustache. He was an expert in martial arts, and I know that because he could beat a person much bigger than him and he could kick a man much bigger than him with his leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there would be the Kardelj group that would come. You mentioned them earlier. Is that the group that you mentioned as being the group of Seselj's men at the Standard factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kardelj was a member of the Loznica group.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Again a leading question and very much off the point. In the statement there is no reference to Kardelj's group. Kardelj is mentioned as one of the men from Loznica, and now the Prosecutor is leading the witness, asking him a leading question, and if the witness is not concentrated then he might have answered yes, he was from Kardelj's group, and I don't think this is admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will have to go up in the transcript but I'm fairly certain that the witness has already said earlier in the transcript that they were Seselj's group, and he also referred to that group as being the group from Kardelj. So I'm not leading the witness. I'm just confirming to make sure that we have in the same portion of the transcript the information to make it easier to read later on.
